strengths: Genuine methodological novelty: combining invisible-Unicode watermarking with a cue/reply split and a ranking test against reserved counterfactual watermarks yields a text-preserving auditing method with a provable FPR bound (FPR ≤ k/K), addressing a real gap versus visible 'copyright traps' and unreliable MIAs.
Clear and well-motivated problem framing, including a thoughtful discussion of the legal context (EU AI Act, ongoing US litigation) that grounds the practical relevance of the work.

The requirements-driven design (text authenticity, scalability, robustness, black-box operability, soundness, completeness) is clearly mapped onto concrete construction choices (syllable/cue/reply structure, cross-bifix-free-like constraints, TTP-issued candidate sets).

Reasonably thorough multi-axis empirical evaluation (collection size, training-set size, number of concurrent watermarks, ranking-based decision test) across two model families and two text domains, with informative per-chunk hit-probability estimates (p, p_FN).

Honest and fairly detailed limitations section covering robustness to normalization/adversarial removal, reliance on a trusted third party, and scope restricted to LoRA fine-tuning, without overselling generality.
Reasonable reproducibility support: open-weight models, explicit hyperparameters/appendix details, and a stated intent to release code and evaluation scripts.
weaknesses: No empirical robustness evaluation against the most obvious and trivial attack: stripping/filtering zero-width Unicode characters, which any moderately aware data curator or platform could apply, would fully defeat the scheme; this is only discussed qualitatively as future work despite being central to real-world viability.

The method requires marking documents prospectively, before any potential misuse; it cannot help authors/rightsholders audit content that has already been published and potentially scraped, which is arguably the dominant real-world use case motivating the paper's legal framing (e.g., existing books/news already used in training).

Evaluation is limited to two 7B open-weight models fine-tuned via LoRA on modest-scale data (≤15k documents); no experiments with larger models, full fine-tuning, RLHF, closed-weight APIs, or realistically sized commercial fine-tuning corpora, which limits confidence that results generalize to the settings the paper motivates (bank chatbots, GPT-scale systems).

Claimed scalability of the watermark space (millions of watermarks) is only a theoretical combinatorial argument; the actual multi-watermark experiments test at most 12 concurrent watermarks and K=100 candidate sets, far short of validating claims about large-scale multi-user deployment or collision behavior at scale.

Limited statistical rigor: most results are averaged over only 5 runs with reported standard deviations but no significance testing, and some described trends (e.g., Poems dataset regurgitation dropping from 28 to 26 as dataset size quadruples) are used to support robustness claims despite being a fairly small, noisy effect.

No direct experimental comparison against the closest existing text-preserving alternative (homoglyph-based watermarks of Wei et al.), leaving the claimed advantages (e.g., degradation with more watermarks) only qualitatively argued rather than empirically demonstrated head-to-head.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with some inconsistencies (e.g., overloaded symbol λ used both as the verification repetition count and, apparently, as a step variable in Algorithm 1's mark procedure), which could hinder reproducibility and comprehension.

Ethical treatment of embedding invisible marks into third-party personal data (e.g., blogs, CVs) without the data subject's consent is acknowledged but not deeply resolved; the paper's own stated goal of empowering individuals to protect their data sits in tension with a technique that itself modifies personal documents' byte-level content without consent frameworks in place.

strengths: The problem formalization (Sec. II) is clear and the paper nicely separates marking and verification requirements (text authenticity, scalability, robustness, soundness, completeness), which gives a crisp frame for evaluation.

The ranking-test-based decision procedure, which compares the published watermark's regurgitation score against a held-out set of counterfactual watermarks, provides a provable FPR≤k/K bound, addressing a real gap in prior MIA/regurgitation-based provenance claims that cannot bound false positives.

The cue/reply split embedded via invisible Unicode syllables is a reasonably creative mechanism for making black-box detection of document-level memorization both low-invasiveness and scalable (large watermark space, multi-user attribution).

Experiments span two models (LLaMA-2-7B, Mistral-7B) and two domains (blogs, poems), and examine multiple relevant axes: watermark-collection size, training-set size, and number of concurrent watermarks, with reasonably detailed hyperparameters (Appendix B) and dataset statistics (Appendix C) supporting reproducibility.

The Discussion section is candid about weaknesses (robustness to normalization/OCR/adversarial stripping, reliance on a trusted third party, scope limited to fine-tuning) and raises relevant legal/ethical considerations around consent and evidentiary standards.

The related-work section provides a reasonably thorough taxonomy of provenance-auditing and text-watermarking techniques, correctly situating the contribution relative to canary-, backdoor-, distribution-, and format-based methods.
weaknesses: Central robustness claim is essentially untested: the core practical threat to any invisible-Unicode scheme is that mainstream text-cleaning/normalization pipelines (e.g., NFKC normalization, HTML sanitization, deduplication tooling) strip or alter zero-width characters; the paper acknowledges this explicitly (Sec. V, footnote 7) but provides no empirical measurement of how much completeness degrades under even mild, non-adversarial preprocessing that is routine in real LLM data pipelines. This significantly undermines the motivating real-world copyright/privacy use case, since actual training corpora are virtually never used in raw, unprocessed form.

The empirical evaluation is conducted entirely in a highly favorable, toy regime: LoRA fine-tuning (not full fine-tuning or pretraining) on only 1,000–15,000 documents with at most two 7B open-weight models. This is far from the scale and training strategies of production LLMs (web-scale pretraining, RLHF, safety alignment, system prompts) that the legal motivation in the introduction specifically targets (e.g., Anthropic/book-training lawsuits), making the claimed significance for real auditing scenarios questionable.

The scheme fundamentally depends on a trusted third party controlling the entire watermark space and issuing candidate sets before publication; this is a strong practical/ deployment limitation for the stated use cases (e.g., auditing already-published books, news articles, or historical blog posts that were never pre-registered with any such authority), which the paper defers entirely to future work without discussing how the approach could realistically bootstrap onto already-public content.

The claim of being 'text-preserving'/non-invasive is somewhat overstated: although the visible glyphs are unchanged, the underlying byte/character sequence is modified, which the paper itself admits can be unacceptable in some settings (Sec. V) and which also makes the technique detectable/removable by any party aware of the scheme simply by stripping non-printing code points, an attack not evaluated despite being the most obvious and trivial countermeasure.

Several of the headline numbers (100% TPR@0% FPR, <0.1% failure rate, 45% detection at 0.33% marked data) are drawn from a small number of configurations/runs (5 runs per setting, a handful of dataset sizes, max 12 unique watermarks), and variability across models/domains is large (e.g., Mistral vs. LLaMA regurgitation rates differ substantially, and one setting dropped from 95% to 72%), suggesting the strong aggregate claims in the abstract may not generalize robustly across models or domains.

The contribution is largely a recombination of known techniques (invisible-Unicode steganography, canary-based memorization probing, and the ranking test adapted from prior MIA-soundness work), with the main novelty being the cue/reply chunking scheme; the conceptual novelty is therefore incremental relative to the cited prior art (e.g., Wei et al.'s homoglyph-based sound watermarks, Carlini's secret sharer canaries, Zhang et al.'s ranking-test framework).

strengths: The cue/reply split using exclusively invisible Unicode characters is an elegant and genuinely text-preserving mechanism that avoids the drawbacks of prior 'copyright trap' or lexical/syntactic watermarking methods that alter visible content.

The paper correctly diagnoses a real gap (MIAs are unreliable/unsound at document granularity; prior canary/trap methods are either visible, require grey-box probability access, or don't scale to many watermarks) and situates the contribution clearly against this literature (Section VI is thorough).

The ranking-test decision procedure with reserved counterfactual watermarks gives a provable FPR bound (k/K) rather than relying on ad hoc thresholds, which is a meaningful methodological strength for 'sound' provenance claims.

Reasonably broad empirical study: two model families, two text domains, systematic ablations over collection size, dataset size, and number of concurrent watermarks, plus an explicit ranking-test validation with over 18,000 challenges yielding 0 false positives.

The limitations section is candid and specific (robustness to normalization/OCR/active adversaries, reliance on a trusted third party, scope restricted to fine-tuning/LoRA), which aids honest assessment of the work's boundaries.
Reasonable attempt at reproducibility: open-weight models, stated hyperparameters (LoRA config, generation settings in Appendix B), and a stated intention to release code/watermark utilities.
weaknesses: Robustness, which is central to the real-world utility of a provenance-auditing tool intended for legal/forensic use, is essentially untested empirically; the paper only cites an anecdotal ChatGPT example and otherwise defers the entire question to future work, while the introduction motivates the method with high-stakes legal/copyright scenarios where adversarial stripping of invisible characters, paraphrasing, or standard text sanitization pipelines (which often strip zero-width characters by default) would plausibly defeat the scheme entirely.

Evaluation is limited to LoRA-based fine-tuning on two relatively small/older 7B models (LLaMA-2-7b, Mistral-7B-v0.1); no results for full fine-tuning, continued pretraining, RLHF, or more current/larger model families, despite the paper's own acknowledgment that this may not generalize across training paradigms.

Scalability claims (watermark space of ~1.86M, 'scales to millions to billions') are not empirically validated beyond K=100 candidate sets and at most 12 concurrent unique watermarks on datasets of only ~1000 fine-tuning documents; the one setting that showed a significant drop (95%→72%) raises concern about how detection degrades at the larger scales the paper claims to support.

The scheme depends on a trusted third party (TTP) for watermark generation/allocation and commitment, which is a nontrivial practical and trust bottleneck for deployment in adversarial legal contexts; this is acknowledged but not addressed beyond a brief mention of blockchains/logs as future work.

The threshold/FPR argument, while theoretically clean, rests on an assumption (invisible marks 'are unlikely to impact the production of subsequent documents by third parties') that is asserted rather than empirically or theoretically substantiated, and the empirical 0/18,810 false positive rate, while encouraging, is from a narrow set of models/domains and cannot be extrapolated to a rigorous universal FPR guarantee in deployment.

The approach necessarily requires marking documents prospectively before any potential training use; it does not address auditing already-published/already-used sensitive or copyrighted content (e.g., books already online), which is one of the central motivating scenarios in the introduction (e.g., the Anthropic book settlement), somewhat narrowing the paper's practical scope relative to its framing.

Dense notation and multiple overlapping embedding/verification algorithms make the method's practical operation (e.g., concrete prompt construction, exact token budget) harder to follow without careful cross-referencing between Section III and the algorithms/appendices.
